newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka government suffers blow on broadcast bill.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka government suffers blow on broadcast bill.

text.p: Sri Lanka's Supreme Court dealt a blow to the government by ruling that a controversial bill to set up a powerful broadcasting authority was unconstitutional, parliament speaker K.B. Ratnayake said on Tuesday.
The bill, introduced in parliament last month, sought to set up a broadcasting authority with wide powers to monitor, regulate and grant operating licences to radio and television broadcasters.

It was seen by opponents as an effort to stifle freedom of speech and was challenged in the Supreme Court by media watchdog the Free Media Movement (FMM), several private broadcasters and the main opposition United National Party (UNP).
Sri Lankan media organisations hailed the ruling as a victory for democracy.
"The opposition to this bill was in the interest of democracy," said Lucien Rajakarunanayake of the FMM.
"We hope the government will give heed to the order of the Supreme Court and withdraw this bill," he told Reuters.

Ratnayake told parliament the Supreme Court had ruled "that some of the provisions of the bill are inconsistent with the provisions of the constitution and the bill as a whole is inconsistent with Article 10 of the constitution".
Article 10 guarantees the fundamental rights of freedom of thought and conscience.
Ratnayake said the ruling meant that in order for the bill to become law, it would need to be passed by a two-thirds majority in parliament, where the government has only a one-seat majority.
The Court's ruling also meant the bill would have to be put to a national referendum, he said.

Members of the UNP, which has 94 seats in Sri Lanka's 225-seat house and without whose support the bill cannot win a two-thirds majority, burnt a copy of the bill outside parliament soon after the decision was announced.

The proposed bill says the annual renewal of broadcasting licences would need backing from the authority's board of directors, who will include senior officials from government departments, including the defence ministry.
It was not immediately clear what the government planned to do with the bill after the ruling. Government spokesmen were not available for comment.
"We need a bill to regulate broadcasting and to represent our interest," said Shan Wickremesinghe, chairman of the TNL Network, a private television and radio broadcast company.
"But this certainly was not it. We need an independent body, looking after the best interests of broadcasting and of broadcasters," Wickremesinghe said.
